steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our NLP paper on the relationship between skill neurons and robustness in Prompt Tuning. Motivate parameter-efficient finetuning and Prompt Tuning, review what is known about skill neurons, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:

- Prompt Tuning: how it works, performance and robustness

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Pretrained large language models (PLMs) have more and more parameters. For example, Roberta-Large has “only” 355 million parameters, while T5-XXL has 11 billion parameters, and LLama-2 up to 70 billion. Finetuning these models for downstream tasks is extremely expensive, both for computation and for storage. Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods were developed to solve this problem. These methods adapt PLMs to downstream tasks by finetuning only a small set of (additional) parameters.

Besides Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA), Prefix Tuning, and P-Tuning, there is also Prompt Tuning, which is one of the state-of-the-art PEFT methods for PLMs. In Prompt Tuning, prompt tokens are prepended to the model input in the embedding space, and only these prepended tokens are learned during finetuning, while the actual model parameters stay frozen. The original authors of Prompt Tuning ran experiments with different T5 model sizes and showed that the performance of Prompt Tuning is on par with conventional finetuning for larger models. They also showed that, besides reducing computational and storage requirements, Prompt Tuning has the advantage of being more robust to domain shifts, because adapting fewer parameters reduces the risk of overfitting.

Researchers have started to look at the effects of Prompt Tuning on PLM activations to understand how it works. In general, it is known that activations in the feed-forward networks (FFNs) of transformers can specialize to encode specific knowledge or concepts. For Prompt Tuning, it was shown that the overlap between the FFN neurons that different prompts activate can predict prompt transferability. More recently, other work on Prompt Tuning showed that the activations of some FFN neurons are highly predictive of the task labels after Prompt Tuning. The authors' analyses indicate that these “skill neurons” are task-specific, essential for task performance, and probably already generated during pretraining.

- Our work
  - connect robustness and skill neurons
  - RoBERTa and T5 (encoder-only vs encoder-decoder), benchmark datasets covering broad spectrum of NLP tasks
  - several prompts per dataset/model (different seeds), identify skill neurons
  - contributions:
    1. tuned prompts transfer to other datasets, incl. domain shifts, if same type of task
    2. AdversarialGLUE: Prompt Tuning not robust to adversarial data
    3. earlier skill neuron analysis only on RoBERTa; replicate, also find skill neurons in (the encoder of) T5
    4. potential link adversarial robustness <-> skill neurons; T5 more robust than RoBERTa; T5 skill neurons consistent between adversarial and non-adversarial data, RoBERTa's not
- Code: https://github.com/LeonAckermann/robust-neurons
- Conclusion
  - more evidence for skill neurons in PLMs
  - Prompt Tuning usually not adversarially robust; robustness may depend on keeping task-relevant skill neurons on adversarial data
  - skill neurons emerge in pretraining, independent of Prompt Tuning -> general relevance for PLMs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Pretrained large language models (PLMs) have more and more parameters. For example, Roberta-Large has “only” 355 million parameters, while T5-XXL has 11 billion parameters, and LLama-2 up to 70 billion. Finetuning these models for downstream tasks is extremely expensive, both for computation and for storage. Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods were developed to solve this problem. These methods adapt PLMs to downstream tasks by finetuning only a small set of (additional) parameters.

Besides Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA), Prefix Tuning, and P-Tuning, there is also Prompt Tuning, which is one of the state-of-the-art PEFT methods for PLMs. In Prompt Tuning, prompt tokens are prepended to the model input in the embedding space, and only these prepended tokens are learned during finetuning, while the actual model parameters stay frozen. The original authors of Prompt Tuning ran experiments with different T5 model sizes and showed that the performance of Prompt Tuning is on par with conventional finetuning for larger models. They also showed that, besides reducing computational and storage requirements, Prompt Tuning has the advantage of being more robust to domain shifts, because adapting fewer parameters reduces the risk of overfitting.

Researchers have started to look at the effects of Prompt Tuning on PLM activations to understand how it works. In general, it is known that activations in the feed-forward networks (FFNs) of transformers can specialize to encode specific knowledge or concepts. For Prompt Tuning, it was shown that the overlap between the FFN neurons that different prompts activate can predict prompt transferability. More recently, other work on Prompt Tuning showed that the activations of some FFN neurons are highly predictive of the task labels after Prompt Tuning. The authors' analyses indicate that these “skill neurons” are task-specific, essential for task performance, and probably already generated during pretraining.

Our work extends the ongoing research on robustness and skill neurons and makes a connection between these two aspects. We run experiments with RoBERTa and T5 to capture the differences between encoder-only and encoder-decoder architectures, and we use various benchmark datasets that cover a broad spectrum of NLP tasks. For each dataset and model we tune several prompts (using different seeds) and identify the skill neurons that go with them. Our main contributions are:

- 1. Like previous research, we find that tuned prompts can be transferred to other datasets, including datasets with domain shifts, as long as these datasets are about the same type of task.

- 2. We use AdversarialGLUE to show that Prompt Tuning is not robust to adversarial data.

- 3. The skill neuron analysis of the earlier work on skill neurons was limited to RoBERTa. We replicate their findings and also identify skill neurons in (the encoder of) T5.

- 4. We find a potential link between adversarial robustness and skill neurons. T5 is more robust to adversarial data than RoBERTa. T5’s skill neurons on adversarial data are relatively consistent with its skill neurons on the corresponding non-adversarial data, but this is not the case for RoBERTa.

Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LeonAckermann/robust-neurons.

To conclude, our study gives additional evidence that skill neurons exist in PLMs. Prompt Tuning usually lacks adversarial robustness, but our findings indicate that how robust a model is against adversarial attacks may depend on whether it can keep its task-relevant skill neurons on adversarial data. Skill neurons already emerge during pretraining and so are independent of Prompt Tuning, which means our results are relevant for PLMs in general.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Pretrained large language models (PLMs) comprise increasingly large numbers of parameters. For example, while Roberta-Large has “only” 355 million parameters [1], T5-XXL has 11 billion parameters [2], and LLama-2 up to 70 billion [3]. Finetuning such models for downstream tasks is extremely expensive in terms of both computation and storage. Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods have been developed to address this problem. These methods adapt PLMs to downstream tasks by finetuning only a small set of (additional) parameters.

Next to Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [4], Prefix Tuning [5], and P-Tuning [6], Prompt Tuning [7] is one of the state-of-the-art PEFT methods for PLMs [8]. In Prompt Tuning, prompt tokens are prepended to the model input in the embedding space, and only these prepended tokens are learned during finetuning, while the actual model parameters are frozen. In experiments with various T5 model sizes, [7] showed that Prompt Tuning performs on par with conventional finetuning for larger models. The authors also demonstrated that, besides reducing computational and storage requirements, Prompt Tuning has the advantage of being more robust to domain shifts, since adapting fewer parameters reduces the risk of overfitting.

To understand how Prompt Tuning works, researchers have started to look at its effects on PLM activations. In general, activations in the feed-forward networks (FFNs) of transformers [9] are known to specialize to encode specific knowledge [10] or concepts [11]. For Prompt Tuning, it has been shown that the overlap between the FFN neurons activated by different prompts can predict prompt transferability [12]. More recently, [13] showed that the activations of some FFN neurons are highly predictive of the task labels after Prompt Tuning. The authors' analyses indicate that these “skill neurons” are task-specific, essential for task performance, and likely already generated during pretraining.

Our work extends ongoing research on robustness and skill neurons and establishes a connection between the two. We run experiments with RoBERTa [1] and T5 [2] to capture differences between encoder-only and encoder-decoder architectures, and use various benchmark datasets covering a broad spectrum of NLP tasks. For each dataset and model, we tune several prompts (using different seeds) and identify the associated skill neurons. Our main contributions are:

- 1. In line with previous research, we find that tuned prompts can be transferred to other datasets, including datasets involving domain shifts, provided these datasets pertain to the same type of task.

- 2. Using AdversarialGLUE [14], we show that Prompt Tuning is not robust to adversarial data.

- 3. [13] ([13]) limited their skill neuron analysis to RoBERTa. We replicate their findings and further identify skill neurons in (the encoder of) T5.

- 4. We establish a potential link between adversarial robustness and skill neurons. T5 shows greater robustness to adversarial data than RoBERTa. While T5’s skill neurons on adversarial data are relatively consistent with its skill neurons on the corresponding non-adversarial data, this is not the case for RoBERTa.

Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LeonAckermann/robust-neurons.

In conclusion, our study offers additional evidence for the existence of skill neurons in PLMs. Although Prompt Tuning typically lacks adversarial robustness, our findings indicate that a model’s robustness against adversarial attacks may depend on its ability to maintain task-relevant skill neurons on adversarial data. Since skill neurons already emerge during pretraining and are thus independent of Prompt Tuning, our results are of general relevance for PLMs.
